prompts: Name one thing your area does that trades along the service–cost line rather than moving it.

prompts: What proportion of shipments were expedited last quarter, and what did it cost?
For the three largest, what was the underlying cause — lead time data, horizon, or a late demand signal?
Take three items: which fulfilment channel does each use, and is it right?
Is any item routed through a node that adds a step without adding pooling or control?

NESR SUPPLY CHAIN TRAINING PROGRAMME
Level 2 — Practitioner
Release 3 · Source and Deliver — worksheet answers

Answers to all ten module tasks. Tasks 1, 6, 9 and 10 are calculations with definite answers, worked in full in sections B to E. The other six ask about your own area. Work the task before reading the answer.
Module 2 — Test a sourcing decision

items: "We have always done it" is not a core competency. The test is whether we are genuinely better at it than the market, and whether the client would recognise it as part of what they are buying.
When cost and capability conflict, the decision belongs above supply chain. That is not an evasion — trading a permanent capability for a recurring saving is a strategic decision.

What supply chain owes that decision is both sides of it: what it saves, and what it costs in capability, with rebuild time and cost quantified. Presenting only the saving is how capabilities get traded away by accident.

blocks.text: Module 3 — Position three suppliers

items: The common mismatch runs the opposite way to what people expect. Organisations treat important suppliers transactionally far more often than they over-invest in unimportant ones — because depth is expensive, so it gets rationed by habit rather than by importance.
Moving rightward requires both sides to want it. A partnership we declare unilaterally is still an ongoing relationship.
If the answer to the fourth question is no, that is the cheapest improvement in this release. Sending a forecast costs an email; a confirmed capacity reservation is worth considerably more.

blocks.text: Module 4 — Move the line

items: Substituting information for inventory is almost always cheapest to start, and the first step is almost always the same: give the people holding buffer stock visibility of what is already in transit toward them.
A great deal of buffer exists purely because nobody can see what is coming.

If the pooling-versus-proximity conflict is resolved case by case by whoever argues hardest, it is not resolved. The resolution is a policy stating which item classes are centralised and which are positioned.

blocks.text: Module 5 — Expediting and channels

items: If you could not answer the first question, you are in the majority. Expediting cost is spread across many shipments, so it is invisible unless somebody deliberately adds it up — and the total is usually what funds the fix.

The most common answer to the fourth question is a base that material passes through out of habit. If it is not stocked, inspected or consolidated there, it is a handling cost and a delay with no offsetting benefit.

blocks.text: Module 7 — Audit the functions

items: Most bases perform three of the seven functions: storage, break-bulk and some assortment. Consolidation and cross-docking are usually available and unused — and both reduce cost rather than adding it.
If slotting was last reviewed when the warehouse was set up, that is a real opportunity. Consumption patterns change constantly; slotting almost never follows, because nobody owns the review.

blocks.text: Module 8 — Profile your movements

items: The value-versus-weight split is the informative one. Air freight is usually a small share of weight and a large share of cost — which is what makes it worth managing closely.

If transport capacity is forecast nowhere, that is normal and it is an opportunity. The demand plan already contains what you need; converting it into expected container or pallet volumes by month is what allows rates to be contracted rather than bought late.

blocks.text: Reading the result

items: The purchase price advantage is 130 dollars a unit — 38%. By the time transport and duty are added, the landed advantage is 74. By the time ongoing costs are included, the net is 54 a unit.
At 600 units a year, a 3.7-year payback on a 120,000 investment is a marginal case rather than an obvious one. It would become attractive at higher volume and unattractive at lower.

blocks.text: The answer is most sensitive to the ongoing cost estimate of 20 dollars a unit — the figure with no data behind it. At 30 a unit the net saving falls to 26,400 and the payback stretches to 4.5 years; at 10 it rises to 38,400 and the payback falls to 3.1 years. Ways to reduce that uncertainty are commercial rather than analytical: run a trial order and measure for six months, ask for references you can call, and build a break clause into the contract.

NET ANNUAL EFFECT

blocks.text: The working

items: Square root law: 3 locations need 900 × √3 = 900 × 1.732 = 1,559 units. 4 locations need 900 × 2 = 1,800 units.
The increase at 3 locations is 659 units. At a landed cost of 60 dollars and a carrying rate of 25%, that costs 659 × 60 × 0.25 = 9,883 dollars a year.
At 4 locations the increase is 900 units, costing 13,500 dollars a year.
Net effect at 3 locations: 45,000 saved, less 24,000 of facility cost, less 9,883 of carrying cost, giving a net gain of 11,117 a year.
Net effect at 4 locations: 55,000 saved, less 36,000, less 13,500, giving a net gain of 5,500 a year.

blocks.text: The recommendation
Three locations. It produces the largest net gain, and the fourth location roughly halves it.

items: The pattern is the important part: each additional location buys less transport saving and costs more in inventory and fixed cost. The returns diminish, and eventually reverse.

Note what the inventory line does. Without it, four locations would look like a 19,000 gain rather than 5,500 — the square root law removes 13,500 of apparent benefit that would otherwise have been invisible.

blocks.text: The service consideration that could override this: if a location exists to put job-critical stock within reach of a rig, the case for it is availability, not cost, and it may be right even when the arithmetic says otherwise. What the calculation does is make the price of that decision visible. Choosing to pay it is legitimate. Not knowing you are paying it is not.
In-transit carrying cost per day  =  400,000 × 20% ÷ 365  =  219.18 dollars
How to use the break-even figure

items: Below about 641 dollars a day, ocean is the cheaper choice overall. Above it, air is.
On freight alone the premium looks like 21,500. Including in-transit inventory it is 16,021 — so a quarter of the apparent gap was being paid in financed inventory rather than in freight.

The break-even converts an argument into a threshold. Instead of debating whether a shipment is urgent, ask a single answerable question: does a day of delay on this item cost more or less than 641 dollars?

blocks.text: Most people find the threshold lower than expected — which means the faster mode is justified more often than the freight rate alone suggests, and less often than the person raising the request believes. Both halves of that sentence matter.
Two things to check in your working

items: VAT is calculated on the CIF value plus the duty, not on the CIF value alone. Calculating it on 272,000 gives 40,800 and understates the cash requirement by 2,856 — which matters, because somebody has to fund it before the goods are released.

The true landed cost is 292,240, not 335,896. VAT is recoverable by a registered business, so it is a cash flow item rather than a cost. Treating it as a cost overstates the cost of importing by about 15% and can distort a sourcing comparison badly — which takes you straight back to module 1.

blocks.text: DAP versus EXW
Under DAP the seller delivers to the named place, bearing carriage and risk to that point. Under EXW the buyer becomes responsible at the seller's premises.

items: We would arrange and pay for carriage from the supplier's factory gate — including the inland leg in their country, where we have no presence.
We would become responsible for export clearance in the seller's country, which is where we have the least ability to act and the least visibility.
Risk would transfer at the factory gate rather than on delivery, so damage in transit becomes ours from the moment the goods are made available.
The quoted unit price would fall, because the seller is doing less — which is precisely how the term quietly transfers cost and risk while appearing to save money.

blocks.text: That last point is the Incoterms lesson in one line. The term is agreed at quotation stage, long before anyone at a border sees it — and a lower price under a term that hands us the risk is not a lower cost.
